sections.title: Bottom line — the United Kingdom's strategic role

inlines.v: The United Kingdom's role in the Allied Industrial Base is as a demand and market anchor: allies count on it more as a buyer of turbines, vehicles and reactor parts than as a supplier. Its core seats in

strategic compacts are led by demand roles, and its main supply contribution is uranium conversion and enrichment. Nationally, no producing step reaches the top quarter of producers, so nothing reads Preserve. The industrial task is to catch up in the vehicle chain, where the anchors are, and to source battery cells and rare-earth materials from trusted partners, with development cooperation adding cell capacity now and preparing rare-earth capacity later. Storage, wind and grid networks need to be built faster. The high fence belongs around gas and oil supply, the rare-earth chain, and the control software of batteries and rooftop inverters.

blocks.title: The United Kingdom's role in the Allied Industrial Base
blocks.alt: Matrix of the United Kingdom's roles in the strategic compacts of the Allied Industrial Base: where it is essential, holds a substitutable role, or relies on trusted partners.

inlines.v: Each row is a strategic compact in which the United Kingdom holds a role or relies on partners. Dark cells are roles allies cannot easily replace; light cells are roles others could fill; dashed cells mark where the United Kingdom relies on trusted partners, orange where allied supply still falls short of what allies need. In the nuclear row, the share printed in the supplier cell is the AIB's share of world imports of reactor parts, a measure of demand, not of supply.

Figure 3 shows an economy that anchors demand across the clean-energy compacts and supplies in few of them. Where it relies on partners for battery materials and cells and for wind, allied supply falls short, so the bargain has to add capacity, not only redirect trade.

Government should change course in several places. First, gas and oil supply are Secure but rank low among the country's recorded measures (

). That shows little industrial-policy attention, not missing stocks, so test stocks and contracts against the rebuild time. Second, deployment policy lags for wind and grid networks. Next, protection runs ahead of the case in Watch steps such as oil refining, grid components and wafers and PV cells, and in EV mineral mining, a Partner step that needs partnership terms instead. In grid metals refining (

), the data cannot tell whether the measures target electrical steel, a Partner layer, or the wider basket. Finally, battery materials refining reads as needing more attention, but on a thin anchor: test the announced projects before adding support.

blocks.text: 4. Meet reactor needs with allied makers and keep enrichment reliable

inlines.v: Reactors combine high need with a doubtful measured base, so meet that need through co-investment and offtake with the nuclear compact's makers,
, rather than a domestic build alone. Keep conversion and enrichment reliable for allies, and verify the capacity behind them before support scales.

blocks.text: 5. Build trusted cell and rare-earth capacity with developing partners

inlines.v: , through development finance, guarantees and offtake. Prepare

over a longer horizon, with project preparation, infrastructure and skills. Leave the coal pairs aside, since allied supply already covers that need. The objective is both an additional trusted supplier and a durable capability in the partner economy.

blocks.text: 6. Accelerate storage, wind and grid while keeping sourcing open

inlines.v: Deploy faster through infrastructure, permitting and procurement, buying from trusted suppliers such as the wind compact's makers,

. Require certified, trusted firmware and remote access for battery systems and distributed PV inverters, and replace untrusted control in the installed base on a deadline. Shift protection from Watch steps, such as grid components and oil refining, to deployment.

at deployment, Accelerate where deployment need reaches
Watch where the step is a large, commoditized yard;
Preserve where Competitive Position is in the top quarter (
Catch Up where the value is high, the position is not, and a capability anchor is corroborated by other evidence;
Partner where supply-chain need is high but there is neither a top-quarter position nor, for a high-value step, a credible pathway;

Named layers inside a step, such as control software or magnets, take their own choice, and a step whose parts sit behind different fences is mixed. A value that rests on market size alone is capped just under the bar. Observed policy never decides a choice.

Some calls rest on low confidence, an engine review flag, a thin capability anchor, a known data artifact or, at deployment, a single indicator of low confidence. They stay on the map but never enter the Bottom line, the Agenda, the policy table or a headline mark.
